chunks: Yunus ibn 'Abd al-Rahman from al-Mufaddal ibn Salih from one of his companions who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: If a man steals and his left hand is crippled (shala'), his right hand is not cut off, nor is his leg cut off, even if he is one-handed (ashal). Then, if he cuts the hand of another man, retribution (qisas) is taken from him, meaning his hand is not cut off for theft, but it is cut off for retribution. The meaning in this report is that we interpret it to mean that when the Imam sees from him, based on the evidence of the situation, the permissibility of pardoning him, if his left hand is crippled, it is permissible for him (to leave the right hand), so that he does not remain without a hand. And if it is not so, then cutting his right hand is obligatory upon him, according to what the first report contained and that which indicates this.

key_terms.أَشَلّ: One-handed or having a missing/crippled hand
key_terms.بِشَاهِدِ الحَالِ: Based on the evidence of the situation/circumstances
key_terms.شَلّاءُ: Crippled or disabled (specifically referring to the left hand in this context)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on cutting the hand of a thief who has a pre-existing disability in one hand?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling in *al-Ishtibār* to clarify the juristic debate regarding whether the right hand is amputated for theft if the left is already disabled (*shalla’*). The text distinguishes between the punitive amputation for theft (*hudud*), which is waived to prevent total loss of utility, and retributive amputation (*qisas*), which applies regardless of pre-existing conditions. This highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the functional purpose of the punishment rather than rigid literalism.
